extracted.intended_audience: astronomers and mathematicians determining comet orbits from observations; advanced readers of celestial mechanics
extracted.subtask_description: Geometric and observational methods to infer comet distances, intermediate positions, and orbital shape (parabolic/conic) from a small number of observations; includes approximation techniques (parabolic fits, finite differences), parallax reasoning, and rules for how many/which observations to take.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comets move in conic sections about the Sun and sweep areas proportional to times
rubrics_metrics.description: Cometas in sectionibus conicis, solis in centro habentibus moveri, & radiis ad solem ductis areas temporibus proportionales describere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propositio XL states that comets move in conic sections with the Sun at the center and that the areas described by lines drawn to the Sun are proportional to the times (Kepler's area law applied to comets). Corollary 1: if comets return, their orbits are ellipses and the periods relate to planetary periods in the sesquiplicate ratio; Corollary 2: orbits are so near parabolas that parabolas may be used without sensible error; use this principle as a primary dynamical model when fitting comet motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocity–distance scaling (subduplicata ratio)
rubrics_metrics.description: Velocitas cometae erit semper ad velocitatem planetæ ... in subduplicata ratione duplae distantiae planetae ... ad distantiam cometae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary 3 of Prop. XL: the comet's velocity at a given heliocentric distance is to the planet's orbital velocity as the subduplicate (square-root) ratio of the planets' distance squared reciprocal — i.e., v ∝ 1/√r. Use this scaling to compute expected diurnal and hourly motions for a comet at given heliocentric distance; numerical examples are provided to obtain diurnal and hourly arc measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabola as a practical approximation for comet orbits
rubrics_metrics.description: Orbes autem erunt parabolis adeo finitimi, ut eorum vice parabolae sine erroribus sensibilibus adhiberi possint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary 2: for most practical computations (especially near perihelion) a parabola closely approximates a cometary conic and can be used instead of the true conic without sensible observational error. This justifies solving for a parabolic trajectory from a small number of observations as a working model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer comet proximity from parallactic effects and apparent acceleration/retardation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex parallaxi annua/diurnâ convincitur cometas supra regiones sublunares aut in regionibus planetarum versari; angulares accelerations/retardations of apparent motion arise from Earth's motion and yield distance information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma IV and following argument: analyze whether a comet appears faster or slower (or retrograde) at different parts of its apparition depending on whether Earth is moving towards or away from it; this apparent change (and the diurnal/annual parallax contributions) gives a means to deduce whether the comet is nearer than planets, among planets, or beyond. Use observed changes in apparent longitude over time, and compare to the expected contribution from Earth's motion, to estimate heliocentric position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance from brightness and apparent diameter
rubrics_metrics.description: Loci distantia colligitur ex lucis quantitate & apparentis diametri: lux diminuit in ratione quadrupla distantiae; dato lumine & diametro apparente datur distantia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: the illumination of a celestial body by the Sun falls off in the duplicate (square) ratio of distance and the apparent diameter also changes; thus, given the comet's apparent brightness and apparent diameter (and a comparison object like a planet), one can estimate the comet's distance by direct proportionalities. Examples: numeric comparisons with Saturn and observed comet diameters/brightness provide concrete ratios (e.g., distance ratios like 4:5 in the example). Account for the coma/fume which can obscure or add reflected light when applying this method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for coma/smoke when using brightness to infer distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscurationem cometarum per fumum copiosum & crassum considerare; corpus obscuratum a fumo propiora ad solem esse debet, et caudae & caput influunt in luce observata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that the dense coma (smoke) around a comet's head can obscure or reflect light, so inferring proximity purely from apparent brightness may be misleading. One must consider how much light is intrinsic to the nucleus vs scattered/reflected by the coma or tail; if much light is concentrated in the nucleus, the nucleus would be extremely bright and the comet must be nearer the Sun. Conversely, extensive coma can make a distant comet appear brighter than it would if only the nucleus were seen. Use tail/coma morphology and temporal changes in brightness to correct distance estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-difference method to construct a parabola through given points (interpolation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sunto puncta A,B,C,D,E,F &c.; demitte perpendicula ad datum rectam, collige differentias primas, secundas, tertias ...: erit ordinata applicata ad curvam parabolae a + dp + h c^ + dr + es + ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma V provides an explicit algorithm for finding a parabolic curve through given sampled ordinates: drop perpendiculars from given curve points to a chosen base line at equal abscissa intervals (or account for unequal intervals by dividing differences accordingly), compute successive finite differences (first, second, third, ...), and form the series (a + bp + cq + dr + ...) to obtain the ordinate at a chosen abscissa. Use this to interpolate positions or to construct a parabola approximating a curve for area/quadrature. The lemma includes the unequal-interval variant (divide differences by interval length).

rubrics_metrics.name: Areas of arbitrary curves can be approximated by area of a parabola through sample points
rubrics_metrics.description: Areas curvarum omnium inveniri possunt quamproxi-me: si parabola per eadem puncta duci intelligatur, area parabolae hujus eadem quamproximè cum area curvae illius quadrandae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary to Lemma V: selecting a parabola through sampled points of any (quadrable) curve gives a close approximation of the curve's area; since the parabola can be geometrically quadrated, this provides a practical quadrature method. Use sufficient sampling points to ensure the parabola matches the curve closely over the region of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpolate a comet's longitude/latitude at an intermediate time from several observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex observatis aliquot locis cometæ invenire locum ejus ad tempus quodvis intermedium datum (Lemma VI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma VI: given five (or more) observed longitudes at known time intervals, apply Lemma V to the five points to compute the parabola's ordinate at the desired intermediate time; that ordinate gives the interpolated longitude (and similarly for latitude). If only three observations are available and the motion is slow and approximately linear, other lemmas offer methods; overall use parabolic interpolation when motion is sufficiently smooth over the interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance on how many observations to use depending on motion amplitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Si longitudinum observatarum parvæ sint differentiae (gradum tantum 4 vel 5), observationes tres vel quatuor sufficerint; si majores differentiae (gradus 10 vel 20), observationes quinque adhiberi debebunt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma VI explicitly prescribes the number of observations needed for reliable interpolation depending on how rapidly the observed longitude changes: small changes → 3–4 observations suffice; larger changes → use 5 observations. This is practical guidance for planning observation campaigns and choosing the interpolation method (parabola fit vs more points).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive rule to obtain a straight line through a point with given segment ratios to two given lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Per datum punctum P ducere rectam BC, cujus partes PB, PC rectis duabus positione datis AB, AC adscisses, datam habeant rationem ad invicem (Lemma VII).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma VII gives a geometric construction: from P draw any line PD to one of the given axes, extend to E so that PE:PD equals the given ratio; draw through A a line parallel to ED; then CP:PB will equal the required ratio. Use this to set up coordinates or to construct proportional sections needed in interpolation or orbit geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate arc-time relation using parabolic chord constructions and tangents
rubrics_metrics.description: If a comet moves on a parabolic arc, points and chords can be constructed so that the chord cut off from the chord AC is proportional to the time to traverse the arc (Lemmas VIII–X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemmas VIII–X give geometric constructions to approximate the time of traversal of a parabolic arc by lengths of chords constructed via chosen auxiliary points (use of tangents at the vertex, selected points S,P, and proportional constructions). Lemma X: choosing S,P such that SP and related segments satisfy given ratios makes the chord AC approximately equal to the arc traversed in the same time if the comet moved uniformly with the velocity it has at SP. Scholium and corollaries give methods for improving accuracy (choose point n beyond a specific point m). Use these constructions to transform a time-determination problem into a length-measure problem for easier geometric solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate gravitational fall to chord/arc relations for time estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: If a comet falling towards the Sun from altitude SN with the gravitational acceleration it would have at SP, then in half the time it would describe a distance equal to the chord length Im (Lemma XI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma XI furnishes a connection between the motion of a comet under solar gravity (as if it were dropped to fall into the Sun) and the chord lengths of a corresponding parabolic arc: the distance fallen in half the time equals a chord length proportional to the square of half the chord etc. Use this relation to relate temporally-measured arc traversal to an equivalent free-fall distance under assumed gravitational law; this provides an alternate computational route to estimate velocities or to convert chord-length constructions into time/distance estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical observational strategy for solving a comet's parabolic orbit from three observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Select three observations approximately equally spaced in time where the comet is moving more slowly than usual; choose the time interval so that the difference to sum ratio matches a criterion (e.g. sum vs days ≈ 600) or place E near M in lemma VIII; if such observations are not available, determine an intermediate position by Lemma VI (Propositio XLI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propositio XLI notes that determining a parabolic trajectory from three observations is difficult in general; therefore choose three observations as equally spaced as practicable and preferably where the comet's motion is slow (to reduce nonlinearity). The author gives a numerical heuristic for choosing the time interval (relations involving sums and differences of times and a target of order 600 days) and suggests if ideal three-observation sets are not available, first interpolate a new position via Lemma VI (parabolic interpolation from five points) and then apply the three-point method. This is prescriptive observational planning guidance.
